qs.q: A surgical resident is evaluating a patient with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain, localized tenderness at McBurney's point, and low-grade fever. Which histologic finding is strictly required to establish the definitive diagnosis of acute appendicitis?
o: Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells
Presence of a calcified faecalith within the lumen
Transmural lymphoid hyperplasia with mucosal ulceration
Neutrophil infiltration of the muscularis propria
qs.e: The histological diagnosis of acute appendicitis requires the infiltration of neutrophils into the muscularis propria. While faecaliths are common inciting factors, their presence alone without neutrophilic muscle infiltration does not confirm active acute inflammation.

qs.q: A 4-year-old child presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever mimicking acute appendicitis, five days after consuming unpasteurized milk. Which pathogenic mechanism is most characteristic of this clinical presentation?
qs.e: Yersinia and certain invasive bacteria cause mesenteric lymphadenitis through local mucosal invasion. Systemic bacteremic spread leads to metastatic foci rather than localized abdominal findings.

qs.q: Which laboratory finding on a Complete Blood Count (CBC) is most expected in a patient presenting with acute appendicitis?
qs.e: A high white blood cell count (leukocytosis) indicates infection, which is commonly seen in patients with acute appendicitis. Other parameters like hemoglobin do not directly point to acute infection.

qs.q: A 23-year-old man presents with acute appendicitis that ruptures shortly after admission. He is taken to the operating room for surgery, and postsurgical cultures reveal Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis, susceptibilities pending. Which of the following provides adequate empiric coverage of these two pathogens?
qs.e: Piperacillin/tazobactam is a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that provides excellent coverage against both gram-negative aerobes (E. coli) and anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis). While the other agents cover E. coli, only piperacillin/tazobactam provides adequate coverage against Bacteroides species, which are common in intra-abdominal infections.
